title: Northwind Outdoor: responsibility centers, ROI, residual income and transfer pricing
judge_role: Chief financial officer (CFO) of NORTHWIND OUTDOOR

difficulty.rationale: ROI, residual income and transfer pricing combined with a people conflict; four tasks fit a 10 minute ICDC role-play.

scenario:
You are to assume the role of corporate controller for NORTHWIND OUTDOOR, a manufacturer of outdoor clothing and gear with two divisions. The chief financial officer (CFO) (judge) has asked you to help settle a conflict between the two division managers and to review how the company measures divisional performance.

Each division manager has full control over the division's sales, costs and operating assets, and earns a bonus based on the return on investment (ROI) of his or her division. The company's minimum required rate of return is 12%.

The Fabric Division weaves technical outdoor fabric. It has the capacity to produce 100,000 yards per year but currently sells only 80,000 yards to outside customers at $14 per yard. Variable production cost is $8 per yard and variable selling cost is $1 per yard. The selling cost is not incurred on transfers to other Northwind divisions.

The Apparel Division needs 20,000 yards of fabric for next year. An outside supplier has offered fabric of the same quality for $13 per yard. The Fabric Division manager insists that Apparel pay the full market price of $14 per yard. The Apparel Division manager says she will buy from the outside supplier instead, and the two managers are no longer speaking to each other.

The Apparel Division manager is also considering a new line of insulated jackets. The line would require an investment of $400,000 and is expected to earn operating income of $80,000 per year. She plans to reject the proposal.

The CFO (judge) wants you to explain the numbers, recommend a fair transfer price and suggest how the company should measure and reward its division managers.

You must:
- Classify the Fabric and Apparel Divisions as responsibility centers and calculate the ROI of each division
- Evaluate the insulated jacket line using both ROI and residual income
- Determine the acceptable range for the transfer price and the effect of the decision on the company as a whole
- Recommend how to resolve the conflict between the two division managers and how to improve the company's performance measures

You will present your analysis to the CFO (judge) in a role-play to take place in the CFO's office. The CFO (judge) will begin the role-play by greeting you and asking to hear your ideas. After you have presented your analysis and have answered the CFO's (judge's) questions, the CFO (judge) will conclude the role-play by thanking you for your work.
tasks: Classify the Fabric and Apparel Divisions as responsibility centers and calculate the ROI of each division
Evaluate the insulated jacket line using both ROI and residual income
Determine the acceptable range for the transfer price and the effect of the decision on the company as a whole
Recommend how to resolve the conflict between the two division managers and how to improve the company's performance measures

judge_questions: Why not just order the Fabric Division to charge $8?
If ROI causes problems, why do so many companies use it?

solution.overview: A strong answer classifies both divisions as investment centers, computes ROI of 15% and 25%, and shows that the jacket line earns 20% (residual income $32,000) but lowers Apparel's ROI, which is why the manager wants to reject it. It then sets a transfer price range of $8 to $13, shows the company saves $100,000 by transferring internally, and recommends residual income, a balanced scorecard and a headquarters transfer pricing policy.

answer: Four responsibility centers: cost (costs only), revenue (revenue only), profit (revenue and costs), investment (revenue, costs and assets)
Both Fabric and Apparel are investment centers because each manager controls sales, costs and operating assets
ROI = operating income / average operating assets
Both divisions beat the 12% minimum required return

by_task.task: Jacket line: ROI and residual income
answer: Project ROI: 80,000 / 400,000 = 20%, well above the 12% hurdle
Apparel ROI with the project: 380,000 / 1,600,000 = 23.75%, down from 25%
The manager rejects a good project to protect her bonus (goal incongruence)
Residual income = 80,000 - (12% x 400,000) = $32,000, positive, so accept
The company is better off if the jacket line is accepted

by_task.task: Transfer price range and company effect
answer: Fabric has 20,000 yards of idle capacity, so no outside sales are lost
Minimum price = variable cost $8 (the $1 selling cost is avoided internally)
Maximum price = outside supplier price $13
Buying outside costs 20,000 x 13 = $260,000; making inside costs 20,000 x 8 = $160,000
Company saves $100,000 by transferring internally at any price from $8 to $13
If Fabric were at full capacity, minimum = 8 + lost contribution of 5 = $13, so the company would be indifferent

by_task.task: Resolving the conflict and improving performance measures
answer: Meet with both managers together and focus on the company's $100,000 gain, not on who wins
Explain that $14 is not the right price because Fabric has idle capacity and saves the $1 selling cost
Suggest a negotiated price in the range, for example $10.50: Fabric earns 20,000 x 2.50 = $50,000 more and Apparel saves $50,000
Have headquarters set a written transfer pricing policy (negotiated, cost-plus or market-based) and review it each year
Add residual income (or EVA) so managers accept any project earning more than 12%, and tie part of each bonus to company-wide profit
Consider a balanced scorecard: financial, customer, internal business process, and learning and growth

judge_question_answers.question: Why not just order the Fabric Division to charge $8?
answer: It removes the Fabric manager's autonomy and hurts motivation
Fabric would earn zero contribution on the transfer, so its profit and ROI would be understated
Better: a negotiated price between $8 and $13 or a cost-plus policy set in advance

judge_question_answers.question: If ROI causes problems, why do so many companies use it?
answer: It is simple, widely understood and uses accounting data the company already has
It lets you compare divisions of different sizes as a percentage
It holds managers responsible for the assets they use
Its weakness (rejecting good projects) is fixed by adding residual income and a balanced scorecard

key_concepts.definition: A part of a business whose manager is held accountable for specific results: costs, revenues, profits or investment.
A responsibility center whose manager controls only costs, such as a maintenance or human resources department.
A responsibility center whose manager is judged mainly on the revenue it brings in, such as a sales department.
A responsibility center whose manager controls both revenues and costs, such as a single store. Profit = revenue - expenses.
A responsibility center whose manager controls revenues, costs and the assets invested; judged by ROI or residual income.
Operating income as a percentage of the assets used to earn it. ROI = operating income / average operating assets.
Income left after charging for the minimum required return on assets. Residual income = operating income - (minimum rate x operating assets).
When a measure makes a manager's best choice differ from the company's best choice, such as rejecting a 20% project to protect a 25% ROI.
The price one division charges another division of the same company for goods or services.
The lowest price the selling division should accept. Minimum = variable cost per unit + lost contribution margin per unit on outside sales (zero with idle capacity).
Comparing only the extra revenues and costs that change with a decision, such as $13 bought outside versus $8 made inside.
A performance system with four perspectives: financial, customer, internal business process, and learning and growth.

notes: ICDC level because the student must connect three tools (ROI, residual income and transfer pricing) and show how a bonus plan creates goal incongruence, then handle a people conflict. Watch for students who say the transfer price must be $14, who forget the $1 selling cost is avoided internally, or who compute ROI on the project alone without showing the drop in Apparel's divisional ROI.

items.label: Differentiate among management accounting responsibility centers

criteria.exceeds: Defines all four responsibility centers (cost, revenue, profit and investment) with what each manager controls, and explains that Fabric and Apparel are investment centers because each manager controls sales, costs and operating assets, which is why they are judged on ROI or residual income.
criteria.meets: Correctly classifies both the Fabric and Apparel Divisions as investment centers because their managers control sales, costs and operating assets.
criteria.below: Names responsibility centers in general terms but classifies the divisions as profit centers or cannot explain why they are investment centers.
criteria.little: Does not classify the divisions, or confuses responsibility centers with departments or products.

items.label: Describe common management accounting performance measures

criteria.exceeds: Calculates ROI of 15% for Fabric and 25% for Apparel, shows the jacket line earns 20% but drops Apparel's ROI to 23.75% while residual income is a positive $32,000, and explains this goal incongruence and how residual income (or EVA) and a balanced scorecard fix it.
criteria.meets: Calculates divisional ROI of 15% and 25%, jacket line ROI of 20% and residual income of $32,000, and concludes the jacket line should be accepted.
criteria.below: Calculates ROI correctly but omits residual income, or computes the project's 20% ROI without showing the drop in Apparel's ROI to 23.75%.
criteria.little: Does not calculate ROI or residual income, or agrees the jacket line should be rejected.

items.label: Explain the role of transfer pricing in managerial accounting

criteria.exceeds: Sets the acceptable range at $8 to $13 per yard, explaining that the minimum is the $8 variable cost because Fabric has 20,000 yards of idle capacity and avoids the $1 selling cost, and adds that at full capacity the minimum would rise to $13 ($8 plus $5 lost contribution).
criteria.meets: States the transfer price range is $8 (variable cost with idle capacity) to $13 (outside supplier price) per yard.
criteria.below: Gets only one end of the range, or includes the $1 selling cost and sets the minimum at $9.
criteria.little: Insists the transfer price must be the full $14 market price, or gives no range.

items.label: Describe marginal analysis techniques and applications

criteria.exceeds: Compares only the costs that change: buying outside costs $260,000 (20,000 x $13) while making inside costs $160,000 (20,000 x $8), so the company saves $100,000 at any transfer price from $8 to $13, and explains that the transfer price only splits that gain between divisions.
criteria.meets: Shows the company saves $100,000 by transferring the 20,000 yards internally instead of buying outside.
criteria.below: Recognizes that internal transfer is better but gives the wrong savings amount or uses the $14 price in the comparison.
criteria.little: Does not compare the incremental costs, or says buying outside is fine for the company.

criteria.exceeds: Proposes meeting with both managers together to focus on the company's $100,000 gain, suggests a negotiated price such as $10.50 so each division gains $50,000, and recommends a written headquarters transfer pricing policy plus bonuses tied partly to company-wide profit.
criteria.meets: Recommends bringing the managers together, explaining why $14 is not the right price, and negotiating a price within the $8 to $13 range.
criteria.below: Suggests a compromise without tying it to the numbers, or simply sides with one manager.
criteria.little: Ignores the conflict between the managers, or suggests letting Apparel buy outside.

items.label: Critical Thinking: Reason effectively and use systems thinking

criteria.exceeds: Connects the ROI based bonus plan to both problems: the Apparel manager rejecting a 20% project and the divisions fighting over a transfer that saves the company $100,000.
criteria.meets: Reasons correctly from the exhibit data to the ROI, residual income and transfer price conclusions.
criteria.below: Reaches conclusions without showing the reasoning, or treats each division's view as the company's view.

items.label: Problem Solving: Make judgments and decisions and solve problems

criteria.exceeds: Gives the CFO clear decisions: accept the jacket line, transfer internally at a negotiated price between $8 and $13, and add residual income and a balanced scorecard to the bonus plan.
criteria.meets: Recommends accepting the jacket line and transferring the fabric internally within the $8 to $13 range.
criteria.below: Gives recommendations that are partly correct or not clearly stated.
criteria.little: Makes no recommendation, or recommends rejecting the jacket line or buying outside.

criteria.exceeds: Explains ROI, residual income and the transfer price range in plain language the CFO can repeat to both managers, in a logical order, with confident and professional delivery.
criteria.meets: Presents the calculations and recommendations clearly and in an organized way.
criteria.below: Presentation is hard to follow, relies on jargon, or skips steps.

items.label: Creativity and Innovation: Show evidence of creativity

criteria.exceeds: Uses a simple visual such as a price line from $8 to $13 showing how a $10.50 price splits the $100,000 gain, and adds ideas like a balanced scorecard with its four perspectives.
criteria.meets: Organizes the information in a way that makes the transfer price and ROI problems easy to understand.
criteria.below: Presents the facts with little effort to make them engaging or easy to follow.
criteria.little: Shows no evidence of creativity or original thought.

items.label: Overall impression and responses to the judge's questions

criteria.exceeds: Answers both questions confidently: forcing an $8 price removes the Fabric manager's autonomy and gives Fabric zero contribution, so a negotiated or cost-plus price between $8 and $13 is better; and ROI is popular because it is simple, compares divisions of different sizes and holds managers responsible for assets, with its weakness fixed by residual income and a balanced scorecard.
criteria.meets: Answers both questions mostly correctly, including why a forced $8 price hurts Fabric's motivation and why ROI is still widely used.
criteria.below: Answers only one question correctly, or gives vague answers.
criteria.little: Cannot answer the judge's questions, or agrees that ordering an $8 price is the best solution.

key_points: Both divisions are investment centers because each manager controls sales, costs and operating assets
Jacket line ROI is 20%, but Apparel's ROI falls from 25% to 23.75%, so the manager rejects a good project (goal incongruence)
Residual income on the jacket line = $80,000 minus (12% x $400,000) = $32,000, positive, so accept
Transfer price range is $8 (variable cost, idle capacity, $1 selling cost avoided) to $13 (outside price)
Transferring internally saves the company $100,000 ($260,000 outside versus $160,000 inside)
Resolve the conflict with a negotiated price such as $10.50, a headquarters transfer pricing policy, residual income and a balanced scorecard
